lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: STAVE FOUR.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: THE LAST OF THE SPIRITS.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Phantom slowly, gravely, silently, approached. When it came near him, Scrooge bent down upon his knee; for in the very air through which this Spirit moved it seemed to scatter gloom and mystery.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was shrouded in a deep black garment, which concealed its head, its face, its form, and left nothing of it visible save one outstretched hand. But for this it would have been difficult to detach its figure from the night, and separate it from the darkness by which it was surrounded.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He felt that it was tall and stately when it came beside him, and that its mysterious presence filled him with a solemn dread. He knew no more, for the Spirit neither spoke nor moved.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “I am in the presence of the Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Spirit answered not, but pointed onward with its hand.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “You are about to show me shadows of the things that have not happened, but will happen in the time before us,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge pursued.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Is that so, Spirit?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The upper portion of the garment was contracted for an instant in its folds, as if the Spirit had inclined its head. That was the only answer he received.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Although well used to ghostly company by this time, Scrooge feared the silent shape so much that his legs trembled beneath him, and he found that he could hardly stand when he prepared to follow it. The Spirit paused a moment, as observing his condition, and giving him time to recover.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: But Scrooge was all the worse for this. It thrilled him with a vague uncertain horror, to know that behind the dusky shroud, there were ghostly eyes intently fixed upon him, while he, though he stretched his own to the utmost, could see nothing but a spectral hand and one great heap of black.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Ghost of the Future!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he exclaimed,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “I fear you more than any spectre I have seen. But as I know your purpose is to do me good, and as I hope to live to be another man from what I was, I am prepared to bear you company, and do it with a thankful heart. Will you not speak to me?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It gave him no reply. The hand was pointed straight before them.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Lead on!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Lead on! The night is waning fast, and it is precious time to me, I know. Lead on, Spirit!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Phantom moved away as it had come towards him. Scrooge followed in the shadow of its dress, which bore him up, he thought, and carried him along.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They scarcely seemed to enter the city; for the city rather seemed to spring up about them, and encompass them of its own act. But there they were, in the heart of it; on ’Change, amongst the merchants; who hurried up and down, and chinked the money in their pockets, and conversed in groups, and looked at their watches, and trifled thoughtfully with their great gold seals; and so forth, as Scrooge had seen them often.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Spirit stopped beside one little knot of business men. Observing that the hand was pointed to them, Scrooge advanced to listen to their talk.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “No,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said a great fat man with a monstrous chin,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I don’t know much about it, either way. I only know he’s dead.”

lines.speaker: The Man
lines.text: “When did he die?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: inquired another.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Last night, I believe.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Why, what was the matter with him?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked a third, taking a vast quantity of snuff out of a very large snuff-box.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I thought he’d never die.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “God knows,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the first, with a yawn.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “What has he done with his money?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked a red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose, that shook like the gills of a turkey-cock.

lines.speaker: The Man
lines.text: “I haven’t heard,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the man with the large chin, yawning again.

lines.speaker: The Man
lines.text: “Left it to his company, perhaps. He hasn’t left it to me. That’s all I know.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: This pleasantry was received with a general laugh.

lines.speaker: The Same Speaker
lines.text: “It’s likely to be a very cheap funeral,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the same speaker;

lines.speaker: The Same Speaker
lines.text: “for upon my life I don’t know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?”

lines.speaker: The Gentleman
lines.text: “I don’t mind going if a lunch is provided,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: observed the gentleman with the excrescence on his nose.

lines.speaker: The Gentleman
lines.text: “But I must be fed, if I make one.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Another laugh.

lines.speaker: The First Speaker
lines.text: “Well, I am the most disinterested among you, after all,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the first speaker,

lines.speaker: The First Speaker
lines.text: “for I never wear black gloves, and I never eat lunch. But I’ll offer to go, if anybody else will. When I come to think of it, I’m not at all sure that I wasn’t his most particular friend; for we used to stop and speak whenever we met. Bye, bye!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Speakers and listeners strolled away, and mixed with other groups. Scrooge knew the men, and looked towards the Spirit for an explanation.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Phantom glided on into a street. Its finger pointed to two persons meeting. Scrooge listened again, thinking that the explanation might lie here.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He knew these men, also, perfectly. They were men of business: very wealthy, and of great importance. He had made a point always of standing well in their esteem: in a business point of view, that is; strictly in a business point of view.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “How are you?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said one.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “How are you?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned the other.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Well!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the first.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Old Scratch has got his own at last, hey?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “So I am told,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned the second.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Cold, isn’t it?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Seasonable for Christmas time. You’re not a skater, I suppose?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “No. No. Something else to think of. Good morning!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Not another word. That was their meeting, their conversation, and their parting.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge was at first inclined to be surprised that the Spirit should attach importance to conversations apparently so trivial; but feeling assured that they must have some hidden purpose, he set himself to consider what it was likely to be. They could scarcely be supposed to have any bearing on the death of Jacob, his old partner, for that was Past, and this Ghost’s province was the Future. Nor could he think of any one immediately connected with himself, to whom he could apply them. But nothing doubting that to whomsoever they applied they had some latent moral for his own improvement, he resolved to treasure up every word he heard, and everything he saw; and especially to observe the shadow of himself when it appeared. For he had an expectation that the conduct of his future self would give him the clue he missed, and would render the solution of these riddles easy.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He looked about in that very place for his own image; but another man stood in his accustomed corner, and though the clock pointed to his usual time of day for being there, he saw no likeness of himself among the multitudes that poured in through the Porch. It gave him little surprise, however; for he had been revolving in his mind a change of life, and thought and hoped he saw his new-born resolutions carried out in this.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Quiet and dark, beside him stood the Phantom, with its outstretched hand. When he roused himself from his thoughtful quest, he fancied from the turn of the hand, and its situation in reference to himself, that the Unseen Eyes were looking at him keenly. It made him shudder, and feel very cold.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They left the busy scene, and went into an obscure part of the town, where Scrooge had never penetrated before, although he recognised its situation, and its bad repute. The ways were foul and narrow; the shops and houses wretched; the people half-naked, drunken, slipshod, ugly. Alleys and archways, like so many cesspools, disgorged their offences of smell, and dirt, and life, upon the straggling streets; and the whole quarter reeked with crime, with filth, and misery.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Far in this den of infamous resort, there was a low-browed, beetling shop, below a pent-house roof, where iron, old rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal, were bought. Upon the floor within, were piled up heaps of rusty keys, nails, chains, hinges, files, scales, weights, and refuse iron of all kinds. Secrets that few would like to scrutinise were bred and hidden in mountains of unseemly rags, masses of corrupted fat, and sepulchres of bones. Sitting in among the wares he dealt in, by a charcoal stove, made of old bricks, was a grey-haired rascal, nearly seventy years of age; who had screened himself from the cold air without, by a frousy curtaining of miscellaneous tatters, hung upon a line; and smoked his pipe in all the luxury of calm retirement.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge and the Phantom came into the presence of this man, just as a woman with a heavy bundle slunk into the shop. But she had scarcely entered, when another woman, similarly laden, came in too; and she was closely followed by a man in faded black, who was no less startled by the sight of them, than they had been upon the recognition of each other. After a short period of blank astonishment, in which the old man with the pipe had joined them, they all three burst into a laugh.

lines.speaker: The First Speaker
lines.text: “Let the charwoman alone to be the first!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried she who had entered first.

lines.speaker: The First Speaker
lines.text: “Let the laundress alone to be the second; and let the undertaker’s man alone to be the third. Look here, old Joe, here’s a chance! If we haven’t all three met here without meaning it!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “You couldn’t have met in a better place,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said old Joe, removing his pipe from his mouth.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Come into the parlour. You were made free of it long ago, you know; and the other two an’t strangers. Stop till I shut the door of the shop. Ah! How it skreeks! There an’t such a rusty bit of metal in the place as its own hinges, I believe; and I’m sure there’s no such old bones here, as mine. Ha, ha! We’re all suitable to our calling, we’re well matched. Come into the parlour. Come into the parlour.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The parlour was the space behind the screen of rags. The old man raked the fire together with an old stair-rod, and having trimmed his smoky lamp (for it was night), with the stem of his pipe, put it in his mouth again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: While he did this, the woman who had already spoken threw her bundle on the floor, and sat down in a flaunting manner on a stool; crossing her elbows on her knees, and looking with a bold defiance at the other two.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “What odds then! What odds, Mrs. Dilber?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the woman.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Every person has a right to take care of themselves. He always did.”

lines.speaker: The Laundress
lines.text: “That’s true, indeed!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the laundress.

lines.speaker: The Laundress
lines.text: “No man more so.”

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Why then, don’t stand staring as if you was afraid, woman; who’s the wiser? We’re not going to pick holes in each other’s coats, I suppose?”

lines.speaker: Mrs. Dilber
lines.text: “No, indeed!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Mrs. Dilber and the man together.

lines.speaker: Mrs. Dilber
lines.text: “We should hope not.”

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Very well, then!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried the woman.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “That’s enough. Who’s the worse for the loss of a few things like these? Not a dead man, I suppose.”

lines.speaker: Mrs. Dilber
lines.text: “No, indeed,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Mrs. Dilber, laughing.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “If he wanted to keep ’em after he was dead, a wicked old screw,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: pursued the woman,

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “why wasn’t he natural in his lifetime? If he had been, he’d have had somebody to look after him when he was struck with Death, instead of lying gasping out his last there, alone by himself.”

lines.speaker: Mrs. Dilber
lines.text: “It’s the truest word that ever was spoke,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Mrs. Dilber.

lines.speaker: Mrs. Dilber
lines.text: “It’s a judgment on him.”

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “I wish it was a little heavier judgment,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: replied the woman;

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “and it should have been, you may depend upon it, if I could have laid my hands on anything else. Open that bundle, old Joe, and let me know the value of it. Speak out plain. I’m not afraid to be the first, nor afraid for them to see it. We know pretty well that we were helping ourselves, before we met here, I believe. It’s no sin. Open the bundle, Joe.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: But the gallantry of her friends would not allow of this; and the man in faded black, mounting the breach first, produced his plunder. It was not extensive. A seal or two, a pencil-case, a pair of sleeve-buttons, and a brooch of no great value, were all. They were severally examined and appraised by old Joe, who chalked the sums he was disposed to give for each, upon the wall, and added them up into a total when he found there was nothing more to come.

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “That’s your account,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Joe,

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “and I wouldn’t give another sixpence, if I was to be boiled for not doing it. Who’s next?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Mrs. Dilber was next. Sheets and towels, a little wearing apparel, two old-fashioned silver teaspoons, a pair of sugar-tongs, and a few boots. Her account was stated on the wall in the same manner.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I always give too much to ladies. It’s a weakness of mine, and that’s the way I ruin myself,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said old Joe.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “That’s your account. If you asked me for another penny, and made it an open question, I’d repent of being so liberal and knock off half-a-crown.”

lines.speaker: The First Woman
lines.text: “And now undo my bundle, Joe,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the first woman.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Joe went down on his knees for the greater convenience of opening it, and having unfastened a great many knots, dragged out a large and heavy roll of some dark stuff.

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “What do you call this?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Joe.

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “Bed-curtains!”

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Ah!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned the woman, laughing and leaning forward on her crossed arms.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Bed-curtains!”

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “You don’t mean to say you took ’em down, rings and all, with him lying there?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Joe.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Yes I do,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: replied the woman.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Why not?”

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “You were born to make your fortune,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Joe,

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “and you’ll certainly do it.”

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “I certainly shan’t hold my hand, when I can get anything in it by reaching it out, for the sake of such a man as He was, I promise you, Joe,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned the woman coolly.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Don’t drop that oil upon the blankets, now.”

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “His blankets?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked Joe.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Whose else’s do you think?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: replied the woman.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “He isn’t likely to take cold without ’em, I dare say.”

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “I hope he didn’t die of anything catching? Eh?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said old Joe, stopping in his work, and looking up.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Don’t you be afraid of that,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned the woman.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “I an’t so fond of his company that I’d loiter about him for such things, if he did. Ah! you may look through that shirt till your eyes ache; but you won’t find a hole in it, nor a threadbare place. It’s the best he had, and a fine one too. They’d have wasted it, if it hadn’t been for me.”

lines.speaker: Joe
lines.text: “What do you call wasting of it?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked old Joe.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Putting it on him to be buried in, to be sure,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: replied the woman with a laugh.

lines.speaker: The Woman
lines.text: “Somebody was fool enough to do it, but I took it off again. If calico an’t good enough for such a purpose, it isn’t good enough for anything. It’s quite as becoming to the body. He can’t look uglier than he did in that one.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge listened to this dialogue in horror. As they sat grouped about their spoil, in the scanty light afforded by the old man’s lamp, he viewed them with a detestation and disgust, which could hardly have been greater, though they had been obscene demons, marketing the corpse itself.

lines.speaker: The Same Woman
lines.text: “Ha, ha!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: laughed the same woman, when old Joe, producing a flannel bag with money in it, told out their several gains upon the ground.

lines.speaker: The Same Woman
lines.text: “This is the end of it, you see! He frightened every one away from him when he was alive, to profit us when he was dead! Ha, ha, ha!”

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Spirit!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge, shuddering from head to foot.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “I see, I see. The case of this unhappy man might be my own. My life tends that way, now. Merciful Heaven, what is this!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He recoiled in terror, for the scene had changed, and now he almost touched a bed: a bare, uncurtained bed: on which, beneath a ragged sheet, there lay a something covered up, which, though it was dumb, announced itself in awful language.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The room was very dark, too dark to be observed with any accuracy, though Scrooge glanced round it in obedience to a secret impulse, anxious to know what kind of room it was. A pale light, rising in the outer air, fell straight upon the bed; and on it, plundered and bereft, unwatched, unwept, uncared for, was the body of this man.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge glanced towards the Phantom. Its steady hand was pointed to the head. The cover was so carelessly adjusted that the slightest raising of it, the motion of a finger upon Scrooge’s part, would have disclosed the face. He thought of it, felt how easy it would be to do, and longed to do it; but had no more power to withdraw the veil than to dismiss the spectre at his side.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Oh cold, cold, rigid, dreadful Death, set up thine altar here, and dress it with such terrors as thou hast at thy command: for this is thy dominion! But of the loved, revered, and honoured head, thou canst not turn one hair to thy dread purposes, or make one feature odious. It is not that the hand is heavy and will fall down when released; it is not that the heart and pulse are still; but that the hand was open, generous, and true; the heart brave, warm, and tender; and the pulse a man’s. Strike, Shadow, strike! And see his good deeds springing from the wound, to sow the world with life immortal!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: No voice pronounced these words in Scrooge’s ears, and yet he heard them when he looked upon the bed. He thought, if this man could be raised up now, what would be his foremost thoughts? Avarice, hard-dealing, griping cares? They have brought him to a rich end, truly!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He lay, in the dark empty house, with not a man, a woman, or a child, to say that he was kind to me in this or that, and for the memory of one kind word I will be kind to him. A cat was tearing at the door, and there was a sound of gnawing rats beneath the hearth-stone. What they wanted in the room of death, and why they were so restless and disturbed, Scrooge did not dare to think.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Spirit!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “this is a fearful place. In leaving it, I shall not leave its lesson, trust me. Let us go!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Still the Ghost pointed with an unmoved finger to the head.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “I understand you,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge returned,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “and I would do it, if I could. But I have not the power, Spirit. I have not the power.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Again it seemed to look upon him.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “If there is any person in the town, who feels emotion caused by this man’s death,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge quite agonised,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “show that person to me, Spirit, I beseech you!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Phantom spread its dark robe before him for a moment, like a wing; and withdrawing it, revealed a room by daylight, where a mother and her children were.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She was expecting some one, and with anxious eagerness; for she walked up and down the room; started at every sound; looked out from the window; glanced at the clock; tried, but in vain, to work with her needle; and could hardly bear the voices of the children in their play.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At length the long-expected knock was heard. She hurried to the door, and met her husband; a man whose face was careworn and depressed, though he was young. There was a remarkable expression in it now; a kind of serious delight of which he felt ashamed, and which he struggled to repress.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He sat down to the dinner that had been hoarding for him by the fire; and when she asked him faintly what news (which was not until after a long silence), he appeared embarrassed how to answer.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Is it good?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “or bad?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: —to help him.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Bad,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he answered.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “We are quite ruined?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “No. There is hope yet, Caroline.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “If he relents,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said, amazed,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “there is! Nothing is past hope, if such a miracle has happened.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “He is past relenting,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said her husband.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “He is dead.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She was a mild and patient creature if her face spoke truth; but she was thankful in her soul to hear it, and she said so, with clasped hands. She prayed forgiveness the next moment, and was sorry; but the first was the emotion of her heart.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “What the half-drunken woman whom I told you of last night, said to me, when I tried to see him and obtain a week’s delay; and what I thought was a mere excuse to avoid me; turns out to have been quite true. He was not only very ill, but dying, then.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “To whom will our debt be transferred?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I don’t know. But before that time we shall be ready with the money; and even though we were not, it would be a bad fortune indeed to find so merciless a creditor in his successor. We may sleep to-night with light hearts, Caroline!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Yes. Soften it as they would, their hearts were lighter. The children’s faces, hushed and clustered round to hear what they so little understood, were brighter; and it was a happier house for this man’s death! The only emotion that the Ghost could show him, caused by the event, was one of pleasure.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Let me see some tenderness connected with a death,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge;

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “or that dark chamber, Spirit, which we left just now, will be for ever present to me.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Ghost conducted him through several streets familiar to his feet; and as they went along, Scrooge looked here and there to find himself, but nowhere was he to be seen. They entered poor Bob Cratchit’s house; the dwelling he had visited before; and found the mother and the children seated round the fire.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Quiet. Very quiet. The noisy little Cratchits were as still as statues in one corner, and sat looking up at Peter, who had a book before him. The mother and her daughters were engaged in sewing. But surely they were very quiet!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “‘And He took a child, and set him in the midst of them.’”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Where had Scrooge heard those words? He had not dreamed them. The boy must have read them out, as he and the Spirit crossed the threshold. Why did he not go on?

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The mother laid her work upon the table, and put her hand up to her face.

lines.speaker: The Same Woman
lines.text: “The colour hurts my eyes,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The colour? Ah, poor Tiny Tim!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “They’re better now again,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Cratchit’s wife.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “It makes them weak by candle-light; and I wouldn’t show weak eyes to your father when he comes home, for the world. It must be near his time.”

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “Past it rather,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Peter answered, shutting up his book.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “But I think he has walked a little slower than he used, these few last evenings, mother.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They were very quiet again. At last she said, and in a steady, cheerful voice, that only faltered once:

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I have known him walk with—I have known him walk with Tiny Tim upon his shoulder, very fast indeed.”

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “And so have I,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Peter.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “Often.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “And so have I,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: exclaimed another. So had all.

lines.speaker: The Same Woman
lines.text: “But he was very light to carry,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she resumed, intent upon her work,

lines.speaker: The Same Woman
lines.text: “and his father loved him so, that it was no trouble: no trouble. And there is your father at the door!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She hurried out to meet him; and little Bob in his comforter—he had need of it, poor fellow—came in. His tea was ready for him on the hob, and they all tried who should help him to it most. Then the two young Cratchits got upon his knees and laid, each child a little cheek, against his face, as if they said,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Don’t mind it, father. Don’t be grieved!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Bob was very cheerful with them, and spoke pleasantly to all the family. He looked at the work upon the table, and praised the industry and speed of Mrs. Cratchit and the girls. They would be done long before Sunday, he said.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Sunday! You went to-day, then, Robert?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said his wife.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “Yes, my dear,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned Bob.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I wish you could have gone. It would have done you good to see how green a place it is. But you’ll see it often. I promised him that I would walk there on a Sunday. My little, little child!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Bob.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “My little child!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He broke down all at once. He couldn’t help it. If he could have helped it, he and his child would have been farther apart perhaps than they were.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He left the room, and went up-stairs into the room above, which was lighted cheerfully, and hung with Christmas. There was a chair set close beside the child, and there were signs of some one having been there, lately. Poor Bob sat down in it, and when he had thought a little and composed himself, he kissed the little face. He was reconciled to what had happened, and went down again quite happy.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They drew about the fire, and talked; the girls and mother working still. Bob told them of the extraordinary kindness of Mr. Scrooge’s nephew, whom he had scarcely seen but once, and who, meeting him in the street that day, and seeing that he looked a little—

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “just a little down you know,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Bob, inquired what had happened to distress him.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “On which,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “for he is the pleasantest-spoken gentleman you ever heard, I told him. ‘I am heartily sorry for it, Mr. Cratchit,’ he said, ‘and heartily sorry for your good wife.’ By the bye, how he ever knew that, I don’t know.”

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “Knew what, my dear?”

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “Why, that you were a good wife,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: replied Bob.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “Everybody knows that!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Peter.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “Very well observed, my boy!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Bob.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I hope they do. ‘Heartily sorry,’ he said, ‘for your good wife. If I can be of service to you in any way,’ he said, giving me his card, ‘that’s where I live. Pray come to me.’ Now, it wasn’t,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “for the sake of anything he might be able to do for us, so much as for his kind way, that this was quite delightful. It really seemed as if he had known our Tiny Tim, and felt with us.”

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I’m sure he’s a good soul!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Mrs. Cratchit.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “You would be surer of it, my dear,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: returned Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “if you saw and spoke to him. I shouldn’t be at all surprised—mark what I say!—if he got Peter a better situation.”

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “Only hear that, Peter,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Mrs. Cratchit.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “And then,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried one of the girls,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “Peter will be keeping company with some one, and setting up for himself.”

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “Get along with you!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: retorted Peter, grinning.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “It’s just as likely as not,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “one of these days; though there’s plenty of time for that, my dear. But however and whenever we part from one another, I am sure we shall none of us forget poor Tiny Tim—shall we—or this first parting that there was among us?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Never, father!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried they all.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “And I know,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I know, my dears, that when we recollect how patient and how mild he was; although he was a little, little child; we shall not quarrel easily among ourselves, and forget poor Tiny Tim in doing it.”

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.text: “No, never, father!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: they all cried again.

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I am very happy,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said little Bob,

lines.speaker: Bob
lines.text: “I am very happy!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Mrs. Cratchit kissed him, his daughters kissed him, the two young Cratchits kissed him, and Peter and himself shook hands. Spirit of Tiny Tim, thy childish essence was from God!

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Spectre,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “something informs me that our parting moment is at hand. I know it, but I know not how. Tell me what man that was whom we saw lying dead?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come conveyed him, as before—though at a different time, he thought: indeed, there seemed no order in these latter visions, save that they were in the Future—into the resorts of business men, but showed him not himself. Indeed, the Spirit did not stay for anything, but went straight on, as to the end just now desired, until besought by Scrooge to tarry for a moment.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “This court,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “through which we hurry now, is where my place of occupation is, and has been for a length of time. I see the house. Let me behold what I shall be, in days to come!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Spirit stopped; the hand was pointed elsewhere.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “The house is yonder,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge exclaimed.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Why do you point away?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The inexorable finger underwent no change.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge hastened to the window of his office, and looked in. It was an office still, but not his. The furniture was not the same, and the figure in the chair was not himself. The Phantom pointed as before.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He joined it once again, and wondering why and whither he had gone, accompanied it until they reached an iron gate. He paused to look round before entering.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A churchyard. Here, then; the wretched man whose name he had now to learn, lay underneath the ground. It was a worthy place. Walled in by houses; overrun by grass and weeds, the growth of vegetation’s death, not life; choked up with too much burying; fat with repleted appetite. A worthy place!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Spirit stood among the graves, and pointed down to One. He advanced towards it trembling. The Phantom was exactly as it had been, but he dreaded that he saw new meaning in its solemn shape.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Before I draw nearer to that stone to which you point,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge,

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “answer me one question. Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of things that May be, only?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Still the Ghost pointed downward to the grave by which it stood.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “Men’s courses will foreshadow certain ends, to which, if persevered in, they must lead,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Scrooge.

lines.speaker: Scrooge
lines.text: “But if the courses be departed from, the ends will change. Say it is thus with what you show me!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Spirit was immovable as ever.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Scrooge crept towards it, trembling as he went; and following the finger, read upon the stone of the neglected grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Last of the Spirits

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Am I that man who lay upon the bed?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he cried, upon his knees.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The finger pointed from the grave to him, and back again.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “No, Spirit! Oh no, no!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The finger still was there.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Spirit!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he cried, tight clutching at its robe,

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “hear me! I am not the man I was. I will not be the man I must have been but for this intercourse. Why show me this, if I am past all hope!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: For the first time the hand appeared to shake.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Good Spirit,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he pursued, as down upon the ground he fell before it:

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Your nature intercedes for me, and pities me. Assure me that I yet may change these shadows you have shown me, by an altered life!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The kind hand trembled.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me. I will not shut out the lessons that they teach. Oh, tell me I may sponge away the writing on this stone!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: In his agony, he caught the spectral hand. It sought to free itself, but he was strong in his entreaty, and detained it. The Spirit, stronger yet, repulsed him.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Holding up his hands in a last prayer to have his fate reversed, he saw an alteration in the Phantom’s hood and dress. It shrunk, collapsed, and dwindled down into a bedpost.
